entries.previousTitle: Systematic Bias – when errors in judgment follow a predictable pattern
entries.title: Systematic Bias – a measurement and statistical concept, not one cognitive bias
entries.description:
Systematic bias is a general measurement and statistical concept. It describes a consistent or predictable tendency for measurements, estimates, or study results to miss a reference or target value. It is not the name of one psychological mechanism.

Where can it show up?
- Measurement: an instrument or procedure consistently pushes values high or low.
- Research: sampling, confounding, measurement, or analysis creates a structural deviation in the result.
- Data pipelines: one mapping, rule, sensor, or transformation repeatedly moves output in the same direction.

A better check
- Define the target or reference value first.
- Measure the direction and size of the deviation instead of treating it as random noise.
- Check calibration, sampling, design, data collection, transformations, and analysis.
- Use validation data or an independent method when possible.
- Do not assume a psychological cause just because the error repeats. Name a specific cognitive mechanism only when evidence supports one.

More observations can reduce random uncertainty, but they do not automatically remove a systematic error built into the process.
entries.reason: The existing reviewed copy correctly separated systematic bias from a standalone cognitive-bias mechanism, but the public presentation still used legacy markers and the controlled taxonomy classified the entry only as a generic phenomenon. This thematic override makes the distinction explicit in plain language.
